Accrual accounting records income and expenses when they happen, not when money moves. If you sell something today but the customer pays next month, accrual shows the sale now. If you get a bill for supplies this week but pay later, accrual records the cost now. This gives a clearer picture of how the business is doing over time.

Cash-basis accounting records income and expenses only when cash is received or paid. Using the same examples, the sale only shows when the payment arrives, and the supply cost only appears when you pay the bill. Cash basis is simpler and can make cash flow obvious, but it can hide whether the business actually earned money or owes bills in a period.

In short: accrual shows activity when it happens (better for understanding performance), while cash basis shows activity when cash changes hands (simpler and focused on liquidity). Choose accrual for accuracy; choose cash basis for simplicity.
